content: Candida vulvovaginitis is an infection that affects the vagina and the vestibule, primarily occurring in women of reproductive age. It is caused by various species of Candida, with Candida albicans being the most common pathogen, followed by other species such as Candida glabrata and Candida krusei. Patients typically present with symptoms such as intense vulvar itching, a burning sensation during urination, and abnormal vaginal discharge. The discharge is often described as thick, white, and resembling cottage cheese. Microscopic examination of the discharge reveals the presence of fungal hyphae and spores, which are diagnostic of the condition. Uncomplicated cases of Candida vulvovaginitis generally respond well to treatment with topical or oral azole antifungal medications. However, approximately 5-8% of women experience recurrent vulvovaginitis, defined as four or more episodes within a year. These cases require a more prolonged treatment regimen, including an induction phase followed by maintenance therapy. The first description of a yeast-like fungus causing human infection was made in 1839 by B. Langenbeck, who identified it in cases of oral thrush. Candida vulvovaginitis can be classified based on the duration of the infection and the specific strain of Candida involved. The pathophysiology of Candida vulvovaginitis involves several virulence factors of Candida species, although the exact mechanism by which asymptomatic vaginal colonization transitions to symptomatic infection remains poorly understood. Genetic predisposition may play a role, as the condition is more common in certain families and among African-American women. Candida species are part of the normal flora in many individuals, but their overgrowth can lead to symptomatic infection. This overgrowth is typically kept in check by the human immune system and the presence of other microorganisms, such as lactic acid-producing bacteria like lactobacilli. Disruption of this balance, whether due to external irritants (e.g., detergents or douches) or internal factors (e.g., hormonal changes, pregnancy, or antibiotic use), can lead to Candida overgrowth. Other risk factors include diabetes mellitus, the use of oral contraceptives, engaging in vaginal intercourse immediately after anal intercourse without proper hygiene, and the use of glycerin-containing lubricants. Hormone replacement therapy and infertility treatments may also predispose individuals to Candida infections. While Candida infections can be transmitted sexually from men to women, transmission from women to men is rare. It is important to differentiate Candida vulvovaginitis from other conditions with similar symptoms, such as bacterial vaginosis, trichomonas vaginitis, and atrophic vaginitis. Epidemiological studies on the prevalence of Candida vulvovaginitis are limited, as it is not a reportable disease. Risk factors for the condition include the use of antibiotics, pregnancy, diabetes, and obesity, all of which create an environment conducive to yeast growth. There are no established screening recommendations for Candida vulvovaginitis. The condition is generally self-limiting and does not lead to complications, although some patients may experience recurrent episodes. It is highly responsive to treatment with local or systemic antifungal agents. The most prominent symptom of Candida vulvovaginitis is pruritus, accompanied by a thick, white vaginal discharge. The thick, whitish discharge may adhere to the vaginal walls. Laboratory diagnosis involves microscopic examination of the discharge using a wet mount or potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation. In cases where the infection does not respond to treatment or recurs frequently, a culture may be performed. Treatment involves the use of antifungal medications, such as amphotericin, clotrimazole, nystatin, fluconazole, and ketoconazole. Surgery has no role in the management of Candida vulvovaginitis, as medical therapy with topical or oral antifungal agents is the standard of care. Primary prevention of Candida vulvovaginitis is not well-established, but wearing cotton underwear may help reduce the risk of infection. For secondary prevention, maintenance therapy with fluconazole may be used to prevent recurrent episodes. Treating male sexual partners with oral ketoconazole does not appear to affect cure or recurrence rates in women with Candida vulvovaginitis.
